His statement—"by mixing"—is a precaution against adjacency. His statement—"what is not purifying"—is a precaution against dirt. His statement—"and water has no need for it"—is a precaution against what flows over it, like quicklime and the like. His statement—"like meat water and bean water"—means their broths. He only analogized to them because Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) disagrees with us on the main question but agrees on these two.

As for his statement—"one of the three qualities of water changes—taste, odor, or color"—and making one quality sufficient to remove purifying power, this is the correct, well-known doctrine that the majority definitively stated in the paths (ṭuruq), and al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) explicitly stated it in al-Buwayṭī and al-Umm; I saw it in both. Al-Mutawallī and al-Rūyānī narrated from al-Shāfiʿī that he said: "Only the change of all three qualities removes purifying power"—this is a strange text. Al-Rāfiʿī narrated that the author of Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ narrated two statements: one, which is the well-known and the choice of Ibn Surayj, is that one quality removes purifying power; the second, which is the narration of al-Rabīʿ, is that color alone removes it, and taste with odor removes it, but if either is alone, it does not—this too is strange and weak.

As for the quality of change: if it is a large change, it removes purifying power definitively. If it is slight—e.g., a little saffron falls in and it yellows slightly, or soap or flour and it whitens slightly, such that it is not attributed to it—then there are two aspects. The correct one is that it is purifying, because the name remains. This is how the Khurāsānians corrected it, and it is the chosen view. The second is that it is not purifying, transmitted by Imām al-Ḥaramayn and others from the Iraqians and al-Qaffāl. Its rationale is analogy to impurity, where there is no difference between a large and slight change. This is answered for the chosen doctrine by saying that the domain of impurity is harsher.

* As for the wording of the chapter: "al-ṭuḥlub" (algae) is with ḍammah on the ṭā' and ḍammah or fatḥah on the lām—two well-known pronunciations. "Al-nūrah" (quicklime) is with ḍammah on the nūn: soft stones with white lines over which water flows and dissolves them. "Al-bāqillā'" (beans) has two pronunciations: one with shaddah on the lām and shortening, written with a yā'; the second with takhfīf on the lām and lengthening, written with an alif. And God knows best.

(Branch)
What we have mentioned—the prohibition of purification with water changed by mixing with what is not purifying, when water has no need for it—is our doctrine, the doctrine of Mālik, Dāwūd, and likewise Aḥmad in the more correct of the two narrations. Abū Ḥanīfah said it is permissible with water changed by saffron and every pure thing, whether the change is slight or large, provided it flows and is not thick—except meat broth and bean broth. This is why the author refuted them with his statement: "like meat water and bean water." This is the author's habit: he points to obliging the opponent with what he agrees upon, so pay attention to that. Al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn narrated in his Taʿlīqah a statement of al-Shāfiʿī like Abū Ḥanīfah's doctrine—this is very strange and weak.

Abū Ḥanīfah's evidence is analogy to algae and the like. Our companions' evidence is the analogy the author mentioned, and they relied upon it. If they say: "Purification with bean water is impermissible only because it became a condiment (udm)," the answer is from two aspects: First, being a condiment has no effect, because if colocynth (ḥanẓal) or other things were cooked in water, purification with it would be impermissible by agreement, even if it did not become a condiment. This shows that being a condiment has no effect; rather, the criterion is the removal of the absolute name of water. Second, this meaning exists in saffron water, for it becomes a dye and a perfume, and it is forbidden for the pilgrim in iḥrām to touch it, and he incurs a ransom (fidyah) for it. As for their analogy to algae, it is weak, because algae is needed and cannot be guarded against, unlike our case. And God knows best.

(Branch)
Our companions—the author of al-Ḥāwī and others—said: "It is the same whether the pure thing mixes with water when the water is two qullas or more; the ruling in all cases is one, as previously stated."

(Branch)
Imām al-Ḥaramayn said: "If a pedantic theologian objects to the jurists regarding their distinction between adjacency (mujāwarah) and mixing (mukhālaṭah), claiming that the contact of saffron is also adjacency, since the interpenetration of bodies is impossible, we say to him: The bases of obligatory rulings are not taken from such avenues, but rather from what people's understanding encompasses, especially in matters built on meaning. There is no doubt that the people of language, linguistically and legally, divided change into adjacency and mixing, even if what is called 'mixing' in absolute terms is in reality adjacency. The consideration is the usage of the tongue."

(Branch)
If one swears not to drink water, and he drinks water changed by saffron or the like, he does not break his oath. If he appoints someone to buy water for him and he buys this, the purchase does not fall to the principal, because the name does not apply to it in absolute terms. The author of al-Bayān mentioned this.

The author (may God have mercy on him) said:
* "If something that does not mix with it falls into it and changes its odor—like fragrant oil and aloeswood (ʿūd)—then there are two statements (qawlān). In al-Buwayṭī, he said: 'Wuḍū' with it is not permissible, like water changed by saffron.' Al-Muzanī narrated that it is permissible, because its change is from adjacency, so it is as if it changed by a carcass near it. If a little camphor falls into it and its odor changes, then there are two aspects: one, wuḍū' with it is not permissible, as if changed by saffron; the second, it is permissible, because it does not mix with it, and it only changes by way of adjacency."

(Commentary)
These two statements are well-known. The correct one among them, by agreement of the companions, is the narration of al-Muzanī that purification with it is permissible. This was definitively stated by the majority of the senior Iraqians, including al-Shaykh Abū Ḥāmid and his two companions al-Māwardī and al-Māḥamalī in his books al-Majmūʿ, al-Tajrīd, and al-Muqniʿ; Abū ʿAlī al-Bandanījī in his book al-Jāmiʿ; al-Shaykh Abū al-Fatḥ Naṣr ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Naṣr al-Maqdisī al-Zāhid in his two books al-Tahdhīb and al-Intikhāb al-Dimashqī; and others. And a group of Khurāsānians from the companions of al-Qaffāl, including al-Shaykh Abū Muḥammad in al-Furūq, al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn, al-Fūrānī, and others. The more correct of the two aspects in the second question is also permissibility.

Know that the first question—the question of the two statements—has no difference in it between whether the change is in taste, color, or odor. This is the correct view. Al-Shaykh Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (may God have mercy on him) said: "In my view, change by adjacency can only occur in odor, because change in color and taste cannot be imagined except by the separation and mixing of particles, whereas odor can occur without that. This is why its odor changes by what is on the surface of the water, but not its taste or color." What al-Shaykh Abū ʿAmr said is weak and rejected; we do not know it from any of the companions except what I will mention from al-Māwardī, God willing. Rather, it contradicts the implication of the companions' speech and their absolute statements, which indicate no difference between the three qualities. Indeed, it contradicts what a group of them explicitly stated, including the leader of the companions, al-Shaykh Abū Ḥāmid, and his companion al-Māḥamalī. Abū Ḥāmid said in his Taʿlīqah, in the chapter on water that becomes impure and that which does not: "If something that does not mix falls into it—like solid aloeswood, ambergris, or fragrant oil—it does not mix, but if it changes some of its qualities, it is purifying." Al-Māḥamalī said in al-Tajrīd: "Al-Shāfiʿī said: 'If a little of what does not mix with it falls into it—like aloeswood, ambergris, and oil—there is no harm.' He said: 'There is no difference between whether it changes the water's qualities or not.'" This is their wording. Their statement "one of its qualities" is explicit regarding what I mentioned. Thus, the correct view is that there is no difference between the qualities.

His statement—"as if it changed by a carcass near it"—means a carcass thrown outside the water, near it. In this case, the carcass does not harm it definitively; rather, the water is purifying without disagreement.

As for his statement—"if a little camphor falls into it and its odor changes, then there are two aspects"—the later scholars have differed over its precise form. Among those who refined it is Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, who said: "Whoever interprets 'camphor' here as solid has erred, because then his statement 'a little' would have no benefit or meaning, and because then it would be the very first question. The correct form is that it is soft (rakhw), but it is so little that it does not appear in the extremities of the water due to its smallness; rather, it is consumed at the place of its fall. If the odor of all of it changes, then it is known that it changed by adjacency, so the two aspects apply, derived from the previous question—the question of the two statements."
